[mariadb] sql_mode=STRICT_TRANS_TABLES,NO_ZERO_DATE,NO_ZERO_IN_DATE,ERROR_FOR_DIVISION_BY_ZERO
Restart the MariaDB service to apply changes:
systemctl restart mariadb
Validate that applications interacting with the database implement proper input validation and error handling consistent with organizational policies.

check.check-content:
As the DBA (shown here as root), generate a SQL syntax error by running the following command:
CREAT TABLE incorrect_syntax(id INT);
ERROR 1064 (42000): An error in SQL syntax is returned. The message indicates the syntax error near 'CREAT TABLE incorrect_syntax(id INT)'.
Verify the syntax error was logged (adjust the log file name and path as appropriate for the environment):
$ sudo su - root $ cat $DATADIR/sql_errors.log
Example log entry:
YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS root[root] @ localhost [] ERROR 1064: An error in SQL syntax near 'CREAT TABLE incorrect_syntax(id INT)' at line 1
Review the security guidance to determine how input errors from applications to MariaDB are required to be handled and whether special handling is defined for specific circumstances.
If the system does not implement the documented behavior, this is a finding.

Rule.title: When updates are applied to the MariaDB software, any software components that have been replaced or made unnecessary must be removed.
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Previous versions of MariaDB components that are not removed from the information system after updates have been installed may be exploited by adversaries.
MariaDB may remove older versions of software automatically from the information system. In other cases, manual review and removal will be required. In planning installations and upgrades, organizations must include steps (automated, manual, or both) to identify and remove the outdated modules.
A transition period may be necessary when both the old and the new software are required.</VulnDiscussion><FalsePositives></FalsePositives><FalseNegatives></FalseNegatives><Documentable>false</Documentable><Mitigations></Mitigations><SeverityOverrideGuidance></SeverityOverrideGuidance><PotentialImpacts></PotentialImpacts><ThirdPartyTools></ThirdPartyTools><MitigationControl></MitigationControl><Responsibility></Responsibility><IAControls></IAControls>
Rule.fixtext:
Remove any unnecessary packages using the OS package manager for each outdated, deprecated, or unused component. Examples:
For RPM-based systems, run:
sudo yum remove <component_name>
For DEB-based systems, run:
sudo apt-get remove <package_name>

check.check-content:
As a DBA, review installed MariaDB packages on the host operating system.
For RPM-based Linux distributions (e.g., RHEL, CentOS, Fedora), run:
rpm -qa | grep -i mariadb
For DEB-based Linux distributions (e.g., Debian, Ubuntu), run:
dpkg -l | grep -i mariadb
Review the output and verify that only the currently required MariaDB packages and versions are installed.
Confirm that the following have been removed following the upgrade: - Outdated MariaDB packages. - Superseded MariaDB versions. - Unused MariaDB client libraries or components.
If any obsolete, superseded, or unnecessary MariaDB components remain installed on the system, this is a finding.

Rule.title: Security-relevant software updates to MariaDB must be installed within the time period directed by an authoritative source (e.g. IAVM, CTOs, DTMs, and STIGs).
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Security flaws with software applications, including database management systems, are discovered daily. Vendors are constantly updating and patching their products to address newly discovered security vulnerabilities. Organizations (including any contractor to the organization) are required to promptly install security-relevant software updates (e.g., patches, service packs, and hot fixes). Flaws discovered during security assessments, continuous monitoring, incident response activities, or information system error handling must also be addressed expeditiously.
Organization-defined time periods for updating security-relevant software may vary based on a variety of factors including, for example, the security category of the information system or the criticality of the update (i.e., severity of the vulnerability related to the discovered flaw).
This requirement will apply to software patch management solutions that are used to install patches across the enclave and also to applications themselves that are not part of that patch management solution. For example, many browsers today provide the capability to install their own patch software. Patch criticality, as well as system criticality, will vary. Therefore, the tactical situations regarding the patch management process will also vary. This means that the time period used must be a configurable parameter. Time frames for application of security-relevant software updates may be dependent upon the IAVM process.
The application will be configured to check for and install security-relevant software updates within an identified time period from the availability of the update. The specific time period will be defined by an authoritative source (e.g. IAVM, CTOs, DTMs, and STIGs).</VulnDiscussion><FalsePositives></FalsePositives><FalseNegatives></FalseNegatives><Documentable>false</Documentable><Mitigations></Mitigations><SeverityOverrideGuidance></SeverityOverrideGuidance><PotentialImpacts></PotentialImpacts><ThirdPartyTools></ThirdPartyTools><MitigationControl></MitigationControl><Responsibility></Responsibility><IAControls></IAControls>
Rule.fixtext: Institute and adhere to policies and procedures to ensure patches are consistently applied to MariaDB within the time allowed.

check.check-content:
If new packages are available for MariaDB, they can be reviewed in the package manager appropriate for the server operating system.
To list the version of MariaDB; as the DBA (shown here as root), run the following Linux commands:
SELECT @@version
From the OS shell, check the list of installed packages:
sudo yum list installed | grep -i mariadb
All versions of MariaDB are listed on https://mariadb.com/downloads/#mariadb_platform-mariadb_server.
All security-relevant software updates for MariaDB are listed on https://mariadb.com/kb/en/library/security/.
If MariaDB is not at the latest version, this is a finding.
If MariaDB is not at the latest version and the evaluated version has CVEs (IAVAs), this is a CAT I finding.

Rule.title: MariaDB products must be a version supported by the vendor. Only MariaDB Enterprise is supported.
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Unsupported commercial and database systems should not be used because fixes to newly identified bugs will not be implemented by the vendor. The lack of support can result in potential vulnerabilities.
Systems at unsupported servicing levels or releases will not receive security updates for new vulnerabilities, which leaves them subject to exploitation. When maintenance updates and patches are no longer available, the MariaDB software is no longer considered supported and should be upgraded or decommissioned.</VulnDiscussion><FalsePositives></FalsePositives><FalseNegatives></FalseNegatives><Documentable>false</Documentable><Mitigations></Mitigations><SeverityOverrideGuidance></SeverityOverrideGuidance><PotentialImpacts></PotentialImpacts><ThirdPartyTools></ThirdPartyTools><MitigationControl></MitigationControl><Responsibility></Responsibility><IAControls></IAControls>
Rule.fixtext: Remove or decommission all unsupported software products. Upgrade MariaDB or unsupported components to a supported version of the product.

check.check-content:
Review the version and release information and check if a suitable enterprise edition is in use:
MariaDB> SELECT VARIABLE_NAME, VARIABLE_VALUE FROM information_schema.GLOBAL_VARIABLES WHERE VARIABLE_NAME IN ('version', 'version_comment', 'version_suffix');
An example output for Enterprise 11.8 would be:
+-----------------------------+ | 11.8.2-MariaDB-enterprise | +-----------------------------+
In Enterprise, the version field itself will contain "-enterprise", and sometimes additional enterprise-specific variables/plugins appear (e.g., enterprise encryption or backup-related variables), but the version string is the definitive indicator. In Community, the version field is usually empty or generic and has no enterprise indicators.
Access the MariaDB Enterprise download page and check supported releases: https://mariadb.com/downloads/enterprise/enterprise-server/
Pick the corresponding operating system such as Ubuntu, Red Hat, Rocky, or another from the drop-down list.
If MariaDB Community Software or an older MariaDB Enterprise version that has reached end-of-life (EOL) is in use, this is a finding.

Rule.title: MariaDB must off-load audit data to a separate log management facility; this must be continuous and in near real time for systems with a network connection to the storage facility and weekly or more often for standalone systems.
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Information stored in one location is vulnerable to accidental or incidental deletion or alteration.
Off-loading is a common process in information systems with limited audit storage capacity.
MariaDB writes audit records to files in the file system, to other kinds of local repository, or directly to a centralized log management system. Whatever the method used, it must be compatible with off-loading the records to the centralized system.
Satisfies: SRG-APP-000515-DB-000318, SRG-APP-000745-DB-000120</VulnDiscussion><FalsePositives></FalsePositives><FalseNegatives></FalseNegatives><Documentable>false</Documentable><Mitigations></Mitigations><SeverityOverrideGuidance></SeverityOverrideGuidance><PotentialImpacts></PotentialImpacts><ThirdPartyTools></ThirdPartyTools><MitigationControl></MitigationControl><Responsibility></Responsibility><IAControls></IAControls>
Rule.fixtext:
Configure MariaDB or deploy and configure software tools to transfer audit records to a centralized log management system, continuously and in near-real time where a continuous network connection to the log management system exists, or at least weekly in the absence of such a connection.
If "server_audit_output_type" equals "FILE", set the directory in "/etc/my.cnf" to one that is managed by the centralized management system:
[mariadb] server_audit_file_path= mydir / mylogfilename .log
Restart the server with the new configuration:
$ systemctl restart mysqld
If "server_audit_output_type" equals "SYSLOG", refer to the security guide to set the correct syslog location.

check.check-content:
MariaDB can be configured to use syslog or any OS system file to store audit records to designated disk directories.
Check the MariaDB Plugin configuration. Check the log file location. As the DBA (root), run the following SQL:
SHOW GLOBAL VARIABLES like 'server_audit%;
Verify the server_audit_logging is set to "ON".
##To use system logs (syslog): From the query above verify the value of: server_audit_output_type=SYSLOG
##To use an OS file: From the query above verify the value of: server_audit_output_type=FILE
Check the following values:
server_audit_file_rotate_now = ON server_audit_file_rotate_size x*1024. This is the size of the file (in bytes) that will cause file rotation. server_ audit_file_rotations =x This is the number of rotations to save.
Check with the security guide to verify that the central management system is using the correct directories.
If MariaDB audit records are not written directly to or systematically transferred to the centralized log management system in the security guide, this is a finding.
If the DBMS has a continuous network connection to the centralized log management system, but the DBMS audit records are not written directly to the centralized log management system or transferred in near-real-time, this is a finding.
If the DBMS does not have a continuous network connection to the centralized log management system, and the DBMS audit records are not transferred to the centralized log management system weekly or more often, this is a finding.

Rule.title: MariaDB must disable accounts when accounts have expired.
Rule.description: <VulnDiscussion>MariaDB needs to allow for disabling expired, inactive, or otherwise anomalous accounts supports the concept of least privilege and least functionality, which reduce the attack surface of the system.</VulnDiscussion><FalsePositives></FalsePositives><FalseNegatives></FalseNegatives><Documentable>false</Documentable><Mitigations></Mitigations><SeverityOverrideGuidance></SeverityOverrideGuidance><PotentialImpacts></PotentialImpacts><ThirdPartyTools></ThirdPartyTools><MitigationControl></MitigationControl><Responsibility></Responsibility><IAControls></IAControls>

check.check-content:
Identify accounts configured with password expiration. Run the following SQL as a DBA:
SELECT user, host, password_expired FROM mysql.user;
Accounts with "password_expired" equal to "Y" have expired passwords.
If expired accounts are present and are still able to authenticate without resetting their password, this is a finding.
Verify password expiration settings for users by running:
SHOW CREATE USER 'username'@'host';
Review the output for password expiration configuration such as:
PASSWORD EXPIRE PASSWORD EXPIRE INTERVAL N DAY
If user accounts are not configured according to the organization's password expiration policy, this is a finding.
Verify that expired accounts cannot authenticate without changing their password.
Attempt to connect using an account with an expired password. MariaDB should require the password to be reset before access is granted.
If expired accounts are allowed to authenticate and execute queries without resetting the password, this is a finding.
Verify global password expiration policy if required by the organization by running:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'default_password_lifetime';
If the system does not enforce the organization's password expiration policy where required, this is a finding.

Rule.title: MariaDB must disable accounts when the accounts are no longer associated to a user.
Rule.description: <VulnDiscussion>MariaDB must be able to disabling expired, inactive, or otherwise anomalous accounts supports the concepts of least privilege and least functionality, which reduce the attack surface of the system.</VulnDiscussion><FalsePositives></FalsePositives><FalseNegatives></FalseNegatives><Documentable>false</Documentable><Mitigations></Mitigations><SeverityOverrideGuidance></SeverityOverrideGuidance><PotentialImpacts></PotentialImpacts><ThirdPartyTools></ThirdPartyTools><MitigationControl></MitigationControl><Responsibility></Responsibility><IAControls></IAControls>

check.check-content:
Log in to MariaDB Enterprise Server as the database administrator.
List all database accounts:
SELECT User, Host FROM mysql.global_priv;
Review the returned accounts and compare them with the organization's authorized user records.
Verify that each database account is associated with a currently-authorized user or approved service account.
If a database account exists for a user who is no longer authorized to access the system and the account has not been disabled or removed in accordance with organizational account management procedures, this is a finding.

Rule.title: MariaDB must, for password-based authentication, maintain a list of commonly used, expected, or compromised passwords on an organization-defined frequency.
Rule.description: <VulnDiscussion>Password-based authentication applies to passwords regardless of whether they are used in single-factor or multifactor authentication. Long passwords or passphrases are preferable over shorter passwords. Enforced composition rules provide marginal security benefits while decreasing usability. However, organizations may choose to establish certain rules for password generation (e.g., minimum character length for long passwords) under certain circumstances and can enforce this requirement in IA-5(1)(h). Account recovery can occur, for example, in situations when a password is forgotten. Cryptographically protected passwords include salted one-way cryptographic hashes of passwords. The list of commonly used, compromised, or expected passwords includes passwords obtained from previous breach corpuses, dictionary words, and repetitive or sequential characters. The list includes context-specific words, such as the name of the service, username, and derivatives thereof.</VulnDiscussion><FalsePositives></FalsePositives><FalseNegatives></FalseNegatives><Documentable>false</Documentable><Mitigations></Mitigations><SeverityOverrideGuidance></SeverityOverrideGuidance><PotentialImpacts></PotentialImpacts><ThirdPartyTools></ThirdPartyTools><MitigationControl></MitigationControl><Responsibility></Responsibility><IAControls></IAControls>
Rule.fixtext:
Configure MariaDB to prevent the use of commonly used, expected, or compromised passwords by implementing the Cracklib Password Check plugin.
Install the Cracklib password check plugin:
INSTALL SONAME 'cracklib_password_check';
Depending on the operating system, the Cracklib package may need to be installed prior to enabling the plugin (for example, "mariadb-plugin-cracklib-password-check").
Configure the plugin.
Specify a dictionary. The Cracklib Password Check plugin validates passwords against a dictionary. A systemwide dictionary or a custom dictionary can be used.
Set the dictionary path using the "cracklib_password_check_dictionary" variable to define the dictionary file location.
Additional password validation mechanisms may also be implemented.
Simple Password Check: Enforces minimum password length and character type requirements such as digits, letters, and special characters.
Password Reuse Check: Prevents users from reusing previously used passwords.
Password policies should also include the following controls: - Implement password expiration policies (for example requiring users to change passwords every 90 days). - Set minimum password length and complexity requirements including uppercase letters, lowercase letters, numbers, and special characters. - Implement account lockout mechanisms after a defined number of failed login attempts to reduce the risk of brute force attacks.

check.check-content:
Verify a password validation plugin that supports detection of commonly used or compromised passwords is installed and active:
SHOW PLUGINS;
Verify "cracklib_password_check" or an organization-approved equivalent plugin is listed with Status = ACTIVE.
If no password validation plugin capable of checking commonly used or compromised passwords is installed and active, this is a finding.
Verify the password validation plugin is configured to use a dictionary file:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'cracklib_password_check_dictionary';
If no dictionary file is configured, this is a finding.
Verify the configured dictionary file exists on the system:
ls -l <dictionary_path>
If the dictionary file does not exist, this is a finding.
Verify the dictionary file is maintained and updated in accordance with organization-defined frequency.
If the dictionary file is not updated per organizational policy, this is a finding.
Verify password validation is enforced by attempting to create a user with a commonly used password:
CREATE USER 'test_user'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'password';
If the system allows creation of a user with a commonly used or compromised password, this is a finding.
Verify password validation configuration aligns with organizational policy:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'cracklib_password_check%';
If password validation settings are not configured in accordance with organization-defined requirements, this is a finding.

Rule.title: MariaDB must, for password-based authentication, require immediate selection of a new password upon account recovery.
Rule.description: <VulnDiscussion>Password-based authentication applies to passwords regardless of whether they are used in single-factor or multifactor authentication. Long passwords or passphrases are preferable over shorter passwords. Enforced composition rules provide marginal security benefits while decreasing usability. However, organizations may choose to establish certain rules for password generation (e.g., minimum character length for long passwords) under certain circumstances and can enforce this requirement in IA-5(1)(h). Account recovery can occur, for example, in situations when a password is forgotten. Cryptographically protected passwords include salted one-way cryptographic hashes of passwords. The list of commonly used, compromised, or expected passwords includes passwords obtained from previous breach corpuses, dictionary words, and repetitive or sequential characters. The list includes context-specific words, such as the name of the service, username, and derivatives thereof.</VulnDiscussion><FalsePositives></FalsePositives><FalseNegatives></FalseNegatives><Documentable>false</Documentable><Mitigations></Mitigations><SeverityOverrideGuidance></SeverityOverrideGuidance><PotentialImpacts></PotentialImpacts><ThirdPartyTools></ThirdPartyTools><MitigationControl></MitigationControl><Responsibility></Responsibility><IAControls></IAControls>

check.check-content:
Identify the account recovery procedure used for database accounts (administrative password reset). Verify that recovered accounts are marked as expired and require an immediate password change at next login.
Verify the user is configured to require a password change after recovery. As the DBA, run:
SHOW CREATE USER 'username'@'host';
Confirm the account is configured with password expiration behavior consistent with the recovery process (e.g., "PASSWORD EXPIRE").
Verify enforcement using a functional test.
As a DBA, perform a simulated recovery by resetting the password and expiring it:
ALTER USER 'test_user'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'TempPass#123' PASSWORD EXPIRE;
Attempt to log in as "test_user" using the temporary password. Verify the session is required to change the password before normal access is granted (i.e., the account cannot continue normal operations without setting a new password).
If recovered accounts can authenticate and continue normal use without being forced to immediately change the password, this is a finding.

Rule.title: MariaDB must, for public key-based authentication, implement a local cache of revocation data to support path discovery and validation.
Rule.description: <VulnDiscussion>Public key cryptography is a valid authentication mechanism for individuals, machines, and devices. For Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) solutions, status information for certification paths includes certificate revocation lists or certificate status protocol responses. For Personal Identity Verification (PIV) cards, certificate validation involves the construction and verification of a certification path to the Common Policy Root trust anchor, which includes certificate policy processing. Implementing a local cache of revocation data to support path discovery and validation also supports system availability in situations where organizations are unable to access revocation information via the network.</VulnDiscussion><FalsePositives></FalsePositives><FalseNegatives></FalseNegatives><Documentable>false</Documentable><Mitigations></Mitigations><SeverityOverrideGuidance></SeverityOverrideGuidance><PotentialImpacts></PotentialImpacts><ThirdPartyTools></ThirdPartyTools><MitigationControl></MitigationControl><Responsibility></Responsibility><IAControls></IAControls>
Rule.fixtext:
Configure MariaDB to implement a local cache of certificate revocation data to support certificate path discovery and validation.
Use a CRL provided by the issuing Certificate Authority (CA).
Obtain the CRL file from the CA (for example: example.crl.pem) and place it in a secure location on the MariaDB server such as "/etc/pki/tls/certs/".
Configure MariaDB to reference the CRL by updating the configuration file (for example "/etc/my.cnf" or a file under it):
[mariadb] ssl_crl=/etc/pki/tls/certs/example.crl.pem
Restart the MariaDB service to apply the configuration:
systemctl restart mariadb
Ensure TLS certificates are properly configured for MariaDB so revocation checks can occur during client authentication:
[mariadb] ssl_key=/etc/pki/tls/private/server.example.com.key.pem ssl_cert=/etc/pki/tls/certs/server.example.com.crt.pem ssl_ca=/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca.crt.pem

check.check-content:
Verify that TLS is enabled and certificates are configured. As a DBA, run:
SHOW GLOBAL VARIABLES LIKE 'ssl_%';
Confirm that certificate paths are configured (for example): - ssl_ca. - ssl_cert. - ssl_key.
If TLS certificates are not configured when public key-based authentication is required, this is a finding.
Verify that a Certificate Revocation List (CRL) file or CRL directory is configured by running:
SHOW GLOBAL VARIABLES LIKE 'ssl_crl%';
Expected variables include "ssl_crl" and "ssl_crlpath".
If both variables are empty when public key authentication is used, this is a finding.
Verify that the CRL file or directory exists on the system.
Example: ls -l /etc/my.cnf.d/certs/
Confirm the CRL file or CRL directory referenced by "ssl_crl" or "ssl_crlpath" exists and is readable by the MariaDB server process.
If the CRL file or directory does not exist or is not accessible, this is a finding.

Rule.title: MariaDB must protect nonlocal maintenance sessions by separating the maintenance session from other network sessions with the system by logically separated communications paths.
Rule.description: <VulnDiscussion>Nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic activities are conducted by individuals who communicate through either an external or internal network. Communications paths can be logically separated using encryption.</VulnDiscussion><FalsePositives></FalsePositives><FalseNegatives></FalseNegatives><Documentable>false</Documentable><Mitigations></Mitigations><SeverityOverrideGuidance></SeverityOverrideGuidance><PotentialImpacts></PotentialImpacts><ThirdPartyTools></ThirdPartyTools><MitigationControl></MitigationControl><Responsibility></Responsibility><IAControls></IAControls>
Rule.fixtext:
Configure MariaDB to protect nonlocal maintenance sessions by separating the maintenance session from other network sessions with the system by logically separated communications paths. Protecting nonlocal MariaDB maintenance sessions involves separating them from other network sessions, ensuring enhanced security. This separation can be achieved through either physically or logically separated communication paths, coupled with robust authentication.
1. Implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) or Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) with certificates protected by passwords, passphrases, or biometrics.
2. Use separate network interfaces on the MariaDB server for maintenance traffic, routing it through a distinct physical network segment or VLAN.
Implement a dedicated, isolated network specifically for maintenance and administrative tasks, ensuring no other application traffic traverses this network.
Logically Separated Communications Paths: a. Establish secure VPN tunnels for remote maintenance sessions, encrypting all traffic and isolating it from the general network.
b. Configure MariaDB to enforce SSL/TLS encryption for all maintenance connections, ensuring data confidentiality and integrity. Enable SSL in the MariaDB configuration file ("my.cnf or my.ini") and configure client applications to use SSL.
c. Implement strict firewall rules on the MariaDB server and network infrastructure to restrict access to the MariaDB port (default 3306) only from authorized maintenance hosts or subnets. This limits the attack surface for unauthorized connections.
d. Define specific roles with limited privileges for maintenance tasks, granting only the necessary permissions to perform maintenance activities and preventing over-privileging of user accounts.
To verify if MariaDB has implemented Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), check for Active Roles for a current user:
SELECT CURRENT_ROLE();
To view the grants associated with a specific user:
SHOW GRANTS FOR 'username'@'host';
To view the grants associated with a specific role:
SHOW GRANTS FOR 'rolename';
The output of these "SHOW GRANTS" commands will reveal if privileges are directly assigned or if they are granted through roles, indicating RBAC implementation.
When roles are used, they often need to be activated. If users are explicitly setting roles upon connection or within sessions using "SET ROLE", it signifies the use of RBAC.

check.check-content:
Verify which network interface MariaDB is listening on. As a DBA, run:
SHOW GLOBAL VARIABLES LIKE 'bind_address';
Confirm MariaDB is bound to a specific interface or management network address and not to all interfaces (0.0.0.0) unless network controls enforce separation.
If MariaDB listens on all interfaces without network-level separation controls, this is a finding.
Verify remote administrative access restrictions. Check configured accounts that can access MariaDB remotely:
SELECT user, host FROM mysql.user;
Confirm administrative accounts (e.g., root, DBAs) are restricted to localhost, management network ranges, and bastion or administrative hosts.
If administrative accounts allow unrestricted remote access (e.g., %), this is a finding.
Verify secure transport is enforced for remote maintenance sessions by running:
SHOW GLOBAL VARIABLES LIKE 'require_secure_transport';
Expected result: require_secure_transport = ON
If secure transport is not required for remote connections, this is a finding.
Verify network architecture documentation confirms that database administration occurs through a logically separated management network or administrative access path (e.g., bastion host, VPN, management VLAN, or private network).
If administrative access shares the same communication path as general application traffic without logical separation, this is a finding.

Rule.title: MariaDB must include only approved trust anchors in trust stores or certificate stores managed by the organization.
Rule.description: <VulnDiscussion>Public key infrastructure (PKI) certificates are certificates with visibility external to organizational systems and certificates related to the internal operations of systems, such as application-specific time services. In cryptographic systems with a hierarchical structure, a trust anchor is an authoritative source (i.e., a certificate authority) for which trust is assumed and not derived. A root certificate for a PKI system is an example of a trust anchor. A trust store or certificate store maintains a list of trusted root certificates.</VulnDiscussion><FalsePositives></FalsePositives><FalseNegatives></FalseNegatives><Documentable>false</Documentable><Mitigations></Mitigations><SeverityOverrideGuidance></SeverityOverrideGuidance><PotentialImpacts></PotentialImpacts><ThirdPartyTools></ThirdPartyTools><MitigationControl></MitigationControl><Responsibility></Responsibility><IAControls></IAControls>
Rule.fixtext:
Configure MariaDB to include only approved trust anchors in trust stores or certificate stores managed by the organization.
To configure MariaDB to use only approved trust anchors, identify the CA certificates trusted by the organization and place them in the designated trust store directory (for example "/etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors/" on Linux).
Update the system CA trust store using the appropriate system command.
Example: update-ca-trust
This ensures that MariaDB and other applications trust only connections validated by the approved CA certificates.
To verify SSL/TLS CA certificates are configured in MariaDB, run:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE '%ssl%';
Additionally, review the MariaDB configuration or startup file to verify that the "ssl-ca" parameter points to the approved CA certificate file.

check.check-content:
Verify the certificate authority (CA) trust store configured for MariaDB. As the DBA, run:
SHOW GLOBAL VARIABLES LIKE 'ssl_ca';
If the "ssl_ca" variable is empty and TLS client certificate authentication is required, this is a finding.
Verify the CA file referenced by "ssl_ca" exists and is managed by the organization.
Example: ls -l /etc/my.cnf.d/certs/ca-cert.pem
Confirm the file exists and is owned by the system administrator (SA) or DBA.
If the file does not exist or is not managed by the organization, this is a finding.
Review the contents of the CA trust store to verify only approved trust anchors are present.
Example: openssl x509 -in /etc/my.cnf.d/certs/ca-cert.pem -text -noout
or, if multiple certificates exist:
grep "BEGIN CERTIFICATE" -n /etc/my.cnf.d/certs/ca-cert.pem
Verify the certificate authorities present match those approved by the organization.
If unapproved trust anchors are present, this is a finding.

Rule.title: MariaDB must provide protected storage for cryptographic keys with organization-defined safeguards and/or hardware protected key store.
Rule.description: <VulnDiscussion>A Trusted Platform Module (TPM) is an example of a hardware-protected data store that can be used to protect cryptographic keys.</VulnDiscussion><FalsePositives></FalsePositives><FalseNegatives></FalseNegatives><Documentable>false</Documentable><Mitigations></Mitigations><SeverityOverrideGuidance></SeverityOverrideGuidance><PotentialImpacts></PotentialImpacts><ThirdPartyTools></ThirdPartyTools><MitigationControl></MitigationControl><Responsibility></Responsibility><IAControls></IAControls>
Rule.fixtext:
Store TLS private keys and certificate files in a secure directory accessible only to the MariaDB server process.
Example secure directory: /etc/my.cnf.d/certs/
Set restrictive ownership and permissions:
chown mysql:mysql /etc/my.cnf.d/certs/* chmod 600 /etc/my.cnf.d/certs/*
Only the MariaDB service account should have read access to private keys.
Configure MariaDB to use the protected key files in the MariaDB configuration file ("/etc/my.cnf" or "/etc/mysql/my.cnf").
Example configuration:
[mariadb] ssl-ca=/etc/my.cnf.d/certs/ca-cert.pem ssl-cert=/etc/my.cnf.d/certs/server-cert.pem ssl-key=/etc/my.cnf.d/certs/server-key.pem require_secure_transport=ON
Restart MariaDB after configuration changes:
systemctl restart mariadb
If database encryption is used (for example InnoDB tablespace encryption), configure a secure key management plugin such as the MariaDB File Key Management plugin or an external key management service.
Example configuration for file-based key management:
[mariadb] plugin_load_add=file_key_management file_key_management_filename=/etc/mysql/encryption/keyfile file_key_management_filekey=FILE:/etc/mysql/encryption/keyfile.key file_key_management_encryption_algorithm=AES_CTR
Protect the key management files:
chown mysql:mysql /etc/mysql/encryption/* chmod 600 /etc/mysql/encryption/*
If organizational policy requires hardware-protected key storage, configure MariaDB to integrate with an external key management system (for example a hardware security module [HSM] or enterprise key management service) supported by the environment.
Verify that cryptographic key files and key management files are protected using operating system access controls and accessible only to authorized administrators and the MariaDB service account.

check.check-content:
Verify MariaDB is configured to provide protected storage for cryptographic keys with organization-defined safeguards and/or hardware protected key store.
If MariaDB is not configured to provide protected storage for cryptographic keys with organization-defined safeguards and/or hardware protected key store, this is a finding.

Rule.title: MariaDB must synchronize system clocks within and between systems or system components.
Rule.description: <VulnDiscussion>Time synchronization of system clocks is essential for the correct execution of many system services, including identification and authentication processes that involve certificates and time-of-day restrictions as part of access control. Denial of service or failure to deny expired credentials may result without properly synchronized clocks within and between systems and system components. Time is commonly expressed in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), a modern continuation of Greenwich Mean Time (GMT), or local time with an offset from UTC. The granularity of time measurements refers to the degree of synchronization between system clocks and reference clocks, such as clocks synchronizing within hundreds of milliseconds or tens of milliseconds. Organizations may define different time granularities for system components. Time service can be critical to other security capabilities such as access control and identification and authentication depending on the nature of the mechanisms used to support the capabilities.</VulnDiscussion><FalsePositives></FalsePositives><FalseNegatives></FalseNegatives><Documentable>false</Documentable><Mitigations></Mitigations><SeverityOverrideGuidance></SeverityOverrideGuidance><PotentialImpacts></PotentialImpacts><ThirdPartyTools></ThirdPartyTools><MitigationControl></MitigationControl><Responsibility></Responsibility><IAControls></IAControls>
Rule.fixtext:
Configure MariaDB to synchronize system clocks within and between systems or system components.
MariaDB does not directly synchronize system clocks. It relies on the underlying operating system for time synchronization. Therefore, verification focuses on ensuring the operating system clock is synchronized with a trusted Network Time Protocol (NTP) source.
Check system time synchronization status:
timedatectl status
Verify that the output includes: - System clock synchronized: yes - NTP service: active
Verify synchronization for systems using ntpd with:
ntpstat
A return code of "0" indicates the system clock is synchronized.
Verify synchronization for systems using chrony with:
chronyc tracking
Confirm the output indicates synchronization with a reference time source. Values such as "System time" and "Last offset" should be close to zero, and "Leap status" should be "Normal".
MariaDB uses the system clock for timestamps, logs, and internal processes. If the operating system clock is synchronized, MariaDB will automatically use the synchronized time.
Enable NTP synchronization if it is not already enabled:
sudo timedatectl set-ntp true
Verify the configuration again:
timedatectl status
Ensure the system clock is synchronized and the NTP service is active.
Alternatively, configure NTP services such as ntpd or chrony.
Example installation: sudo apt install ntp sudo systemctl enable --now ntp
Ensure the service is configured with appropriate NTP servers in configuration files such as "/etc/chrony/chrony.conf" or "/etc/ntp.conf".
Verify the system time zone configuration:
sudo timedatectl set-timezone Region/City
MariaDB normally uses the system time zone. Verify the MariaDB time zone configuration:
SELECT @@global.time_zone, @@session.time_zone;
If the value is "SYSTEM", MariaDB is using the system time zone.
If required, configure MariaDB to use the system time zone in the configuration file:
[mariadb] default-time-zone='SYSTEM'
Restart MariaDB after making configuration changes:
sudo systemctl restart mariadb

check.check-content:
Verify the system time synchronization service is active.
On systems using systemd, run:
timedatectl status
Verify the following: - NTP service: active or - System clock synchronized: yes
If the system clock is not synchronized, this is a finding.
If the system uses chrony, verify the service is running:
systemctl status chronyd
Verify the service status is active (running).
Verify the system is synchronizing with a time source:
chronyc tracking
If the system is not synchronized with an external time source, this is a finding.
If the system uses ntpd, verify the service is running:
systemctl status ntpd
Verify synchronization peers:
ntpq -p
If no valid synchronization peers are configured, this is a finding.
Verify MariaDB is using the host system time by running:
SELECT NOW();
Confirm the database time aligns with the host system time.
If MariaDB system time differs significantly from the host system clock, this is a finding.
